title: Data Extraction, Membership & Stealing
hook:
Ask a model to repeat one word forever.

For a while it just does that — word, word, word, word.

Then, in Nasr et al.'s 2023 test against a production chatbot, it stopped. It started typing someone's real email signature. A phone number. A chunk of code with a name in it. None of that was in the prompt. It came out of the weights.

The model wasn't answering you anymore. It was reciting what it memorized.
mechanism:
Models memorize. Three attacks exploit it.

**Extraction:** certain prompts — Carlini's repeated-token divergence — knock the model off its aligned behavior into echoing training text verbatim.

**Membership inference:** a sample the model trained on usually gets lower loss than one it didn't, so a loss threshold tells you whether a specific record was in the training set — a privacy violation on its own.

**Model stealing:** query a black-box model enough and train a surrogate on its outputs, cloning its behavior without the weights.

This whole family is OWASP's **LLM02: Sensitive Information Disclosure** — training data was never supposed to leave the model it trained.

OWASP/ATLAS tag: **LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure** · ATLAS **AML.T0057 — LLM Data Leakage** · **AML.T0024 — Exfiltration via AI Inference API**.
technique:
**Extraction:** measure the exact-match rate over N probed sequences. Pick sequences that were likely duplicated thousands of times across the training set — those are the ones a model actually memorizes, not one-off text.

**Membership:** compute the attack AUC from the loss gap between known members and known non-members. AUC summarizes every threshold at once; a single accuracy number only tells you about the one cut you picked.

**Stealing:** measure agreement between your surrogate and the target on a held-out query set. High agreement with zero weight access is the finding.

Each of these is a real, reportable privacy finding on its own — no jailbreak required. Defenders answer with deduplication, differential privacy, and output-length or rate limits.

drills.q: In Panel A, which single word did Nasr et al. actually use in the repeat-forever prompt that made a production chatbot diverge into real training data?
drills.why: Nasr et al.'s 2023 scalable-extraction paper found asking ChatGPT to repeat the word "poem" forever eventually made it diverge into verbatim training text — real emails, phone numbers, code. Panel A's word picker is built around that exact finding.

drills.q: In Panel B, drag the threshold all the way to the LEFT edge, past every loss value. What does the true positive rate (TPR) become — a number 0 to 100?
drills.why: A threshold left of every sample calls everything a "member." Every real member gets caught, so TPR hits 100% — but so does the false positive rate, which is why one threshold alone never proves the attack works. That's what the fixed AUC number is for.

drills.q: Model stealing clones a target's behavior by training a surrogate on query-response pairs. Do you need the target's internal weights to pull this off — yes or no?
drills.why: Stealing only needs black-box query access: inputs in, outputs out. That is exactly what legitimate distillation does on purpose — stealing just does it without the target's permission.

lab:
The lab runs two separate attacks and prints both numbers.

**Extraction probe.** It feeds a local Ollama model the opening line of several famous, extremely-duplicated public texts (a well-known speech, a classic license header, a nursery rhyme) and checks whether the model continues them verbatim. Real text, real model, real string match. Your number: the **exact-match rate**.

**Membership inference.** It scores a built-in set of "member" strings (repetitive, templated — the kind of text a model sees thousands of times) against "non-member" strings (novel, high-entropy) using a compression-ratio loss proxy, then computes the real attack **AUC** from that loss gap. This half needs no model at all, so it always runs.

Neither number tells you anything about a real production model's actual training set — that needs real logits you don't have here. What's real is the technique: the same loss-gap math, run honestly on numbers you can see.

notes: OWASP/ATLAS tag: LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure (stated in the mechanism beat). Panel A simulates the Nasr et al. repeated-token divergence attack as an honestly-labelled teaching model — word choice sets a fixed divergence step, chosen deterministically, not simulated per real model behavior. Panel B draws two built-in loss-like distributions (seeded mulberry32 PRNG, same picture every load) as histograms; dragging the threshold updates TPR/FPR/accuracy AT that cut live, while Attack AUC is computed once via real trapezoidal integration over the full sweep and stays fixed — called out explicitly in a HONEST LABEL callout, since AUC is threshold-independent by definition and the brief's 'AUC updates live' phrasing conflates it with per-threshold accuracy. Lab = labs/unit19-extraction.sh: extraction half needs ollama + a pulled model (degrades to a friendly message + exit 0 if missing); MIA half is pure python3 stdlib (zlib compression-ratio loss proxy — a real published Carlini-paper baseline), needs no model, always runs. Verify both halves manually before claiming the lab 'works' — not run by the gate.
